subject: chemistry
title: Intermolecular forces
key_idea: Intermolecular forces act between molecules and are much weaker than covalent bonds. There are three types: London forces, permanent dipole–dipole forces and hydrogen bonds. The stronger the forces between molecules, the higher the melting and boiling points.

blocks.text: Intermolecular forces are weak attractions between molecules. This section covers how each of the three types arises.

rows: Electrons move, giving a temporary dipole. This induces a dipole in a neighbouring molecule, and the two attract.
The δ+ end of one molecule attracts the δ− end of another.
Between molecules with H bonded to N, O or F
A strong dipole–dipole attraction between the δ+ H atom and a lone pair on N, O or F in a neighbouring molecule.

items: London forces are also called induced dipole–dipole, instantaneous dipole–induced dipole or id-id forces.
London forces increase with the number of electrons, because a bigger electron cloud is more easily distorted.
Hydrogen bonds need an H atom attached to N, O or F, and a lone pair on an N, O or F atom of the other molecule.
The H–N, H–O or H–F bond is highly polar, because N, O and F are small and very electronegative.
In general, ionic, covalent and metallic bonds are much stronger than intermolecular forces.

diagram.alt: A sorting activity. Sort the substances by the strongest type of intermolecular force between their molecules.
diagram.prompt: What is the strongest type of intermolecular force?

items: London forces act between all molecules and grow with the number of electrons.
Permanent dipole–dipole forces act between polar molecules.
Hydrogen bonds need H bonded to N, O or F.

blocks.text: Melting and boiling a molecular substance only overcomes the forces between molecules. This section covers the trends you need to explain.

items: Alkane boiling points rise with chain length, because longer molecules have more electrons and a larger surface in contact, so the London forces are stronger.
A branched alkane boils at a lower temperature than its straight-chain isomer. The molecules are more compact, have less surface contact and pack less closely, so the London forces are weaker.
An alcohol boils at a higher temperature than an alkane with a similar number of electrons, because it has hydrogen bonds as well as London forces.
HCl, HBr and HI rise in boiling point as the number of electrons increases and the London forces strengthen.
HF has the highest boiling point of the hydrogen halides, because it forms hydrogen bonds.
Stronger intermolecular forces mean a higher boiling point.
More electrons strengthens London forces. Branching weakens them.
Hydrogen bonding raises the boiling point sharply.

sections.heading: Hydrogen bonding in water, ammonia and hydrogen fluoride

blocks.text: Hydrogen bonding explains the unusual properties of water. This section covers how it forms and what it does.

items: In H₂O, each O atom has two lone pairs and two H atoms, so each molecule can make up to four hydrogen bonds.
In liquid NH₃ and liquid HF, hydrogen bonds form between the δ+ H atom and the lone pair on N or F of a neighbour.
A hydrogen bond is drawn as a dotted line from the H atom to the lone pair, in a straight line with the covalent bond. The angle at H is 180°.
Analogous molecules that have H bonded to N, O or F, such as alcohols, amines and carboxylic acids, also hydrogen bond.
Water has high melting and boiling points for its small size, because extra energy is needed to break the hydrogen bonds.
Ice is less dense than liquid water. In ice each molecule is held in an open lattice by four hydrogen bonds, so the molecules are further apart.
When ice melts the lattice collapses and the molecules move closer together.
Water also has a high surface tension, because the hydrogen bonds pull surface molecules inwards.
Hydrogen bonding gives water high melting and boiling points.
Ice floats because hydrogen bonds hold the molecules in an open lattice.

checks.q: Explain how London forces arise between non-polar molecules.
checks.a: The electrons in a molecule move, giving a temporary dipole. This induces a dipole in a neighbouring molecule, and the opposite charges attract.

checks.q: Explain why ethanol has a higher boiling point than propane, which has a similar number of electrons.
checks.a: Ethanol molecules form hydrogen bonds between the δ+ H of the O–H group and the lone pair on O of another molecule. Propane has only London forces. More energy is needed to overcome hydrogen bonds.

checks.q: Explain why ice is less dense than liquid water.
checks.a: In ice each molecule forms hydrogen bonds with four others in an open lattice. The molecules are further apart than in liquid water.

blocks.text: Intermolecular forces help you choose a solvent. A solute dissolves best when the new forces it forms with the solvent are about as strong as those it loses.

items: Water dissolves some ionic compounds, because its polar molecules hydrate the ions. The δ− O atoms surround cations and the δ+ H atoms surround anions.
Water dissolves simple alcohols, because the alcohol forms hydrogen bonds with water.
Water is a poor solvent for compounds such as halogenoalkanes, even though they have polar bonds. They cannot form hydrogen bonds with water.
Non-aqueous solvents dissolve compounds that have similar intermolecular forces to the solvent.
Van der Waals' forces is the generic term for all intermolecular forces, which are the forces between molecules other than those from bond formation.
The types are instantaneous dipole–induced dipole (id-id) and permanent dipole–permanent dipole (pd-pd) forces. Hydrogen bonding is a special case of pd-pd.
Hydrogen bonding is limited to molecules containing N–H and O–H groups, with NH₃ and H₂O as the examples.
